newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian business conditions still subdued-NAB.
newsitem.headline: Australian business conditions still subdued-NAB.

text.p: Australian business conditions remained relatively subdued in the June quarter, consistent with underlying growth of 2.5 to three percent, the latest National Australia Bank (NAB) quarterly business survey has found.

The NAB said that in aggregate terms, trading conditions improved slightly during the second quarter of 1997, but profitability performance deteriorated a little further and there was continued job shedding.
Conditions across sectors and states remain mixed, NAB said.
"Construction, transport and storage and property services have turned around over recent quarters and are improving modestly," NAB chief economist Alan Oster said in a statement.
Financial and personal and recreational services continued to perform relatively well, and there was a marked improvement in retailing mainly due to better trading conditions.

"Manufacturing and wholesaling continue to perform poorly," Oster said, adding that mining, a previously good performer, had reported poor conditions in the quarter for the first time since late 1995.

On a state basis, Victoria and Queensland experienced small improvements, while Western Australia reported poor conditions for the first time since mid-1993. The weakest conditions continued to be experienced in South Australia, NAB said.
The NAB survey also included a measure of current business conditions, and found it less optimistic than the traditional measure based on future expectations.
In the June quarter, "actual" confidence was negative three, compared with expectations of 14 points in the previous survey.
Confidence for the September quarter eased to 10 points, reflecting deterioration in small and medium sized firms.

The survey found conditions were expected to improve in the third quarter, but Oster noted that this may be too optimistic given current activity levels, continued de-stocking intentions and subdued forward orders.
Employment fell in the quarter, against expectations.
"Current labour shedding is also more pronounced in large businesses - with the latter indicating that further downsizing is expected over the next year," Oster said.
Labour costs growth fell to 0.7 percent from over one percent, moderating in all sectors except construction and financial services.
However, there remain concerns about wage pressures over the next year in construction and transport and storage.

About 40 percent of respondents covering about 70 percent of employees in the survey, expected to complete wage agreements in the next year, with wages expected to rise by 3.5 percent. Firms in construction anticipated outcomes of five percent or more.
Overall, a weakish labour market is expected to prevent any generalised wage pressures, and firms anticipate sizeable productivity offsets in wage agreements.
Further out, output and profitability conditions are expected to improve over the next year, but not employment.

Moderation in June quarter price pressures to 0.07 percent, from 0.24 percent in March, together with reported poor profitability levels indicated a continuing economy wide squeeze on margins, and pointing to a good quarterly inflation result NAB said.
After the survey, NAB had lowered its GDP forecast for 1997/98 (July/June) to 3.25 percent from 3.5 percent.

Although NAB expects the second half of calendar 1997 to be stronger than the first half, short-term weakness in activity is seen keeping the unemployment rate around 8.75 percent, before it falls progressively in 1997/98.
Inflation will remain subdued in 1997, but underlying inflation will be rising in 1998 and wage pressures were unlikely to fall below four percent, NAB said.
NAB also said official interest rates were likely to be cut from their current 5.5 percent level in the next month, before heading moderating higher during 1998.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
